title: The scramble for the Middle East
gist: In a long interview about his book 'The Cauldron', Simon Sebag Montefiore argues the modern Middle East's borders were contingent, not inevitable, that most of its states are new creations that could still fragment, and that the region's theatres are now converging from South Europe to South Asia into an entity he calls 'Samastia'. His sharpest working claim is that the real contest is not Islam versus secularism but open versus closed Islam - and that the West should back the open version militarily, on the ISIS-campaign model rather than the Iraq-invasion model.

themes.theme: The 1900 baseline and who actually held power

insights.claim: In 1900 most of the Middle East was ruled from Constantinople by Sultan Abdul Hamid II, whose Ottoman Empire had governed the region since 1517 and at its height stretched from Budapest to Baghdad.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Grounds the region's current borders as roughly a century old against four centuries of single-empire rule - the current map is the anomaly, not the norm.
insights.locator: When it opens in 1900

insights.claim: Having lost its European possessions and Christian subjects, the Ottoman Empire recast itself as an explicitly Islamic state under Abdul Hamid II, who used ethnic and sectarian tension to repress over a million Armenians, close to half a million Greeks, Assyrians and Maronites.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Territorial loss driving a turn to religious-identity consolidation and minority repression is a recurring imperial failure mode worth watching in contemporary multi-ethnic states.
insights.locator: It became an Islamic empire

insights.claim: Britain controlled the Trucial States, Oman, Aden and the coast up to Kuwait indirectly through the Indian Raj, never taking direct control and leaving them self-ruling - which Montefiore identifies as one of the reasons for their success right up to today.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Links today's Gulf state stability and institutional continuity to a light-touch protectorate model rather than direct colonial rule - a structural argument for Gulf durability.
insights.quote: the British never actually took direct control of them, they were self-ruling. That is one of the reasons for their success right up to today.
insights.locator: Moving further east, the eastern and southern coasts

insights.claim: Egypt began the scramble for Africa when its ruler conquered Sudan in 1820 as an empire and a source of slaves - inverting the standard European-origin narrative of African partition.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: A corrective to purely Euro-centric colonial framing that also explains the depth of Egyptian claims in Sudan, now a 12-power battleground.
insights.quote: So ironically, the Egyptians had started the scramble for Africa.
insights.locator: One interesting touch is that Egypt had its own empire

themes.theme: Who is actually to blame for the modern map

insights.claim: The Ottomans had 400 years to govern the Middle East and ended in what was essentially a genocide, so the conclusion is that it is not only Western powers that find the region difficult to govern.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the dominant Sykes-Picot-blame framing that underpins much contemporary regional politics and decolonial analysis.
insights.quote: But the Ottomans had had 400 years to rule the Middle East and ended up in what was essentially a genocide. So one has to conclude that it’s not just Western powers that find the Middle East difficult to govern.
insights.locator: Looking back, we can see that the British, French, and Americans

insights.claim: The British and French mandates - the new name for colonies - actually ruled their Middle Eastern territories for only around 30 years, yet have taken a disproportionate share of blame for everything since.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: A duration argument that reframes the causal weight assigned to European rule in regional dysfunction.
insights.quote: They’ve taken a lot of blame for what’s happened since, but it’s interesting because they actually only ruled them for around 30 years.
insights.locator: The British and French were more successful in the Levant

insights.claim: The post-WWI plan was to give half of Turkey to the Greeks as a new Byzantine Empire, keep Constantinople for the allies and hand eastern Turkey to the Kurds and Armenians, leaving Turks only a small central remnant - a design destroyed by Mustafa Kemal's war on all fronts, culminating in the defeat of the Greeks in 1922.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that imposed partition schemes can be overturned entirely by determined local military action - a template relevant to any externally drawn settlement today.
insights.locator: They decided they would give half of Turkey to the Greeks

insights.claim: The Young Turk faction of Talat, Enver and Jamal were ultra-nationalist eugenicists who believed in social Darwinism and embraced a proto-Nazi Turkish supremacism, and it was under wartime siege that they turned to genocide of Christian minorities.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Genocide here follows from ideology plus existential military pressure - a two-factor model for identifying escalation risk in ethnically stratified states at war.
insights.quote: They were incredibly tough ultra-nationalists who really embraced a sort of proto-Nazi Turkish supremacism.
insights.locator: When the First World War came

insights.claim: Iraq was assembled from three Ottoman vilayets, Libya from two or three, Lebanon and Syria were carved by the French from a Greater Syria they had considered splitting five or six ways - meaning nearly every Middle Eastern state is a 20th-century invention with ancient names.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: State fragility in the region is architectural rather than accidental; assume borders are contingent when modelling long-horizon regional risk.
insights.quote: They had ancient names like Palestine, Syria, Lebanon, and Iraq, but they were new.
insights.locator: Just as there’d never been a Turkish republic

themes.theme: Contingency and the states that could still break

insights.claim: Libya is in civil war and may well break into two countries, Tripoli and Benghazi, reverting to the Ottoman vilayet structure it was assembled from.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Libyan partition is a live scenario with direct implications for oil production control and Mediterranean migration routes.
insights.quote: It could also be two, Tripoli and Benghazi. It may well break into two countries.
insights.locator: A good example is Libya now

insights.claim: Lebanon's confessional one-state design has failed because the Iran-backed Hezbollah militia captured and degraded the state to the point of bankruptcy and chaos, and if restoration fails Lebanon could ultimately split into sectarian entities.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Militia capture is the specific mechanism of Lebanese state failure; watch disarmament and state-restoration progress as the leading indicator for Lebanese risk.
insights.locator: Another example would be Lebanon

insights.claim: Syria's new president Ahmed Al-Sharaa, a former ISIS emir, is attempting to build the united Syria the French originally wanted, and if he fails the country risks breaking into an Alawite state on the Mediterranean coast and a Druze state in the south.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Syrian unity is a single-leader bet; failure would redraw the eastern Mediterranean coastline politically and reopen refugee flows.
insights.locator: Similarly with Syria, the new president of Syria

insights.claim: Had ISIS's leaders not been exhibitionist psychopaths, Montefiore believes no one would have bothered to stop them, and a huge new state would now sit between Syria and Iraq - meaning the group was defeated by its own performative atrocity rather than by the inherent limits of its project.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: A disciplined, non-theatrical jihadist state-builder could succeed where ISIS failed - a substantially more unsettling risk model than the usual reading.
insights.quote: Had its leaders, led by Al-Baghdadi, not been such total psychopaths and exhibitionist psychopaths, no one would have bothered to stop them, I believe.
insights.locator: For example, the rise of ISIS after the Arab Spring

insights.claim: Iraq's survival is credited to its federal concession allowing the Kurds a self-ruling autonomous zone in the north, offering a working model for holding artificial states together despite Iran-linked Shia militia dominance elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Federalism as a cheaper alternative to partition - the template to look for if Syria or Libya are to be held together.
insights.quote: Maybe that is a way that Iraq can keep working as a state in the future.
insights.locator: Iraq now, and I don’t want to hold it up

insights.claim: Measured against the formation of Turkey in 1922-23, the Iran-Iraq war or the American war in Iraq, the Arab-Israeli conflict was a comparatively tiny conflict until October 7th - its Western salience derives from the Holy Land's religious and cultural hold, not its scale.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Explains a persistent mispricing of attention: Western political bandwidth on the region is allocated by religious-cultural salience rather than by casualties or strategic weight.
insights.quote: But the real reason for its intractability and its status in the West is that the Holy Land is a cultural and religious obsession and remains so to this day.
insights.locator: The reason why it’s so intractable

insights.claim: Because Israel's creation coincided with Arab independence, the Arab League states began their independent life with a massive military defeat and used the 750,000 Palestinian refugees as a political pawn, with a dedicated UN organisation in effect preserving rather than resolving their refugee status.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Identifies institutional incentives that entrench the refugee question, implying diplomatic solutions must address the preserving institutions, not just the parties.
insights.quote: They used the Palestinian Arab people, the 750,000 refugees, half of them who had fled, half of them who had been driven out by the Israelis, as a political pawn and prevented them from ever settling anywhere.
insights.locator: But it’s made a lot worse by the fact

insights.claim: A future two-state solution would work better with some federal relationship between a Palestinian entity and a larger Arab state such as Jordan, echoing the historical plans in which King Abdullah of Jordan would rule the Palestinian Arab areas.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: A specific structural variant of two-state that periodically resurfaces in negotiations - worth tracking as a signal of serious diplomacy versus performative process.
insights.locator: I believe that a future two-state solution

insights.claim: For roughly 20 to 25 years a majority of both Israelis and Palestinians wanted compromise and believed in a negotiated settlement, but after October 7th and Israel's Gaza campaign both nations are deeply traumatised and it will take a long time before they recover.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Sets a multi-year, not multi-month, horizon for any realistic peace process - a constraint on regional normalisation timelines and related investment theses.
insights.quote: both nations are deeply traumatised and enraged. It will take a long time before they recover.
insights.locator: But one has to recognise that after October 7th

themes.theme: From pan-Arabism to the battle within Islam

insights.claim: Nasser's pan-Arabism peaked with the 1956 Suez seizure and the 1958 Egypt-Syria union before collapsing through overreach - a police state at home, a poison-gas war in Yemen and finally the Six-Day War defeat - leaving a ten-year ideological vacuum.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Ideological regimes collapse through military overreach rather than argument, and the succeeding ideology takes roughly a decade to form - a timing model for post-regime transitions.
insights.quote: But in fact, he overreached.
insights.locator: In 1956, Nasser was able to take control of the Suez Canal

insights.claim: The 1979 Iranian Islamic Revolution supplied the replacement narrative by co-opting features of Arab nationalism into an anti-Western radical Islamism, and although Iran is Shiite it caused a Sunni version of that radicalism to surge across the region.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Cross-sectarian ideological contagion means containing Iran does not by itself contain Sunni radicalism - relevant to how regional security settlements are scoped.
insights.locator: When it did, it was the 1979 Iranian Revolution

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia is currently leading a war to destroy the Houthis which may end in the collapse of the Houthi regime or at least their retreat to mountainous redoubts - an active front in the battle for the heart of Islam.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Houthi collapse would materially change Red Sea shipping risk; this is a directly monitorable and tradeable regional variable.
insights.quote: Saudi Arabia, representing the opposite approach to Islam, is leading a war now to destroy the Houthis, which may lead to the collapse of the Houthi regime
insights.locator: As we speak, part of that is playing out in Yemen

insights.claim: The regional contest is a small-scale version of a planetary struggle between the open world represented by America and the closed world represented by Russia, China and Iran, and is partly a battle for access to the Straits of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Explicitly ties the sectarian conflict to Hormuz transit risk, the channel through which regional politics transmits to oil prices.
insights.quote: It reflects the wider planetary struggle between the open world represented by America and the closed world represented by Russia, China, and Iran.
insights.locator: This battle for the heart of Islam is going on right now

insights.claim: Citing Nadim Shehadi, the West has misread the struggle as one between Islam and secularism when it is actually between liberal and radical forms of Islam, with the open version traceable to the Umayyad and Abbasid empires rather than being a modern import.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Reframes Western policy from containment of a religion to support for one faction within it - a very different set of partners and instruments.
insights.quote: We see it as a struggle between Islam and secularism, when really it is between liberal and radical forms of Islam.
insights.locator: You cite the Lebanese scholar Nadim Shehadi

insights.claim: The policy contrast is explicit: the Iraq invasion unleashed an insurgency and was a bad model, while the anti-ISIS campaign - Western air power with Kurdish and other militias doing the fighting - defeated ISIS soundly and is the good model.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: A reusable intervention doctrine: enablement over occupation, which predicts the shape of future Western military involvement in the region.
insights.quote: A good example is the campaign against ISIS, where the Americans and the West provided air power, but the fighting was done by Kurdish and other militias, and they defeated ISIS pretty soundly.
insights.locator: A bad example was the Gulf War

insights.claim: Emirati officials have said they do not even want their children studying in British universities because Britain is a hotbed of Islamism, showing that Gulf states now judge Western domestic policy toward Islamism and act on that judgement.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: A direct commercial consequence for UK higher education and a signal that Gulf soft-power and student flows are contingent on Western domestic policy.
insights.quote: ‘We don’t even want our children to study in British universities because Britain is a hotbed of Islamism.’
insights.locator: In our own societies, we need to be vey careful

insights.claim: The Middle East's theatres are converging - Pakistani troops in Arabia, Israeli troops in the UAE, Ukrainian advisers on the ground, and twelve powers backing different factions in Sudan - so the region can no longer be analysed as a discrete geopolitical unit.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Conflict spillover is now cross-continental; regional risk models scoped to the traditional Middle East will systematically understate contagion.
insights.quote: If you look at what’s happening in East Africa and Sudan, there are 12 powers fighting in Sudan now, backing different factions.
insights.locator: The Middle East right now is seeing the convergence of many theatres

insights.claim: Realignment is running along new axes: Saudi Arabia and Turkey are moving closer to Pakistan, India is moving closer to Israel, Turkey and Greece face off in the Eastern Mediterranean, and Israel is getting closer to Greece.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: A concrete alignment map for pricing defence procurement, energy corridors and Eastern Mediterranean gas disputes.
insights.quote: Saudi Arabia and Turkey are moving closer to Pakistan. India is moving closer to Israel, as Turkey and Greece face off in the Eastern Mediterranean, and Israel is getting closer to Greece.
insights.locator: If you look at what’s happening in Arabia

insights.claim: Montefiore proposes 'Samastia' - Southeast Europe, Middle East, West Asia, East Africa - because existing terms such as 'Swana' and 'West Asia' fail to capture a zone now stretching from South Europe to South Asia.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Analytical categories lag reality; redrawing the regional unit of analysis is a prerequisite for correctly scoping exposure in this zone.
insights.quote: So I suggested ‘Samastia’ – Southeast Europe, Middle East, West Asia, East Africa.
insights.locator: We need a new word for that
